SATOM 1.3

An operator console for when the web interface is down, a Service Monitor with per-policy traffic, two years of monitoring history, honest health badges and alerts, and an installer that works on openSUSE.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-08-02 · All releases

In short#

This is a large release with five themes:

  • Operator console. A command-line console, satom, lets you inspect, diagnose and repair a node when its web interface is down. It includes twelve built-in recovery runbooks.
  • Service Monitor. A new monitoring page shows traffic for each appliance and each server policy, and keeps two years of history.
  • Health and alerts that tell the truth. The health badge can now turn red, device alerts send mail when the badge does, and failing automations raise their own alerts.
  • Monitoring in every ADOM. Monitoring is available in each ADOM and stays within it.
  • openSUSE support. The installer has been fixed for openSUSE, and there is a new offline bundle for openSUSE and SLES.

The internal names of the database and the service account also change, which existing installations must migrate. See Before you upgrade.

What's new#

The operator console (satom)#

A console for when the web interface is down#

The new satom command works like the command line on the appliances SATOM manages. It has four kinds of command: get, show, diagnose and execute.

  • Help and modes. Type ? at any point to list the options. You can run a single command (handy for scripts) or open an interactive prompt.
  • It still works when SATOM is broken. The console depends only on the basic system, so it can report on a node even when the application itself is broken.
  • Who can run what. Any user can run get, show and diagnose. execute needs root, and if you are not root it refuses clearly instead of crashing.
  • It cannot be tampered with. It is installed in a protected location that the web application cannot change, and it is reinstalled after every code update.
  • A deeper code check. diagnose python checks that every part of the application can actually load, including parts that load only when needed. This catches a kind of fault that once shipped while SATOM started normally and its health check passed.

39 more commands#

Commands are grouped around the problems SATOM has actually had:

  • Status reads for the automated work that has no page of its own:
  • the four backup copies side by side
  • the scheduler and the timers
  • device and monitoring status
  • whether alerts actually reach anyone
  • jobs, git, users and update history
  • disk, time and certificates
  • Checks:
  • whether the node is armed or merely installed
  • whether each service runs the code on disk
  • the scheduler, the services, the configuration, the web server, git and certificate issuance

diagnose all combines 24 checks into one result in about 3.5 seconds. - Actions: - seed the scheduled actions - restore the database and back up the repository - repair jobs and temporary files - reset or unlock an administrator - run, enable or disable the scheduler - switch maintenance on or off, enable or disable SATOM, restart everything - build a support bundle

Twelve built-in runbooks#

satom show runbook gives step-by-step recovery guides for:

  • the web interface down
  • the database down
  • an idle scheduler
  • a stuck update
  • an expired certificate
  • a full disk
  • peer problems
  • promoting a standby
  • restoring
  • a fresh install
  • being locked out
  • an unreachable device

They are built into the console, not kept on a wiki or website, because the person who needs them usually has no browser and no internet route.

Seeding the scheduled actions#

SATOM never creates scheduled actions for you. A fresh node can do everything, protects nothing, and still looks healthy while it takes no backups at all. satom execute seed actions closes that gap:

  • It first prints what it would create.
  • It applies the plan only when you add --yes.
  • It never changes an existing action, so your own edits always win.

The full command list and output options#

  • satom show tree (or tree) prints every command as a tree. A mark shows the commands that need root and the ones that are destructive. It can also print a flat list, limit the depth, show only root or destructive commands, or produce JSON. It is built from the commands that actually exist, so it is always complete.
  • Output options. You can turn colour on or off, use plain ASCII, or set the width. On a terminal the output is decorated; through a pipe it carries no colour codes and nothing is cut off, and the content is the same either way.

Monitoring#

Service Monitor#

Runtime traffic monitoring has its own page: Monitoring → Service Monitor, available in all four ADOMs.

  • Which page has which probes. Service Monitor has the four traffic probe types: sessions, per-policy sessions, throughput and transactions. Deep monitors keeps the five that look inside the appliance: HTTPS, interface, CPU, memory and the proxy daemon.
  • One page per probe. A probe belongs to exactly one page, and each page only shows, edits and runs its own probes.
  • The same tools on both pages. Both pages share the same charts, history and controls, so they always match.

Traffic probes that need no SSH#

Four new probe types read live figures from a FortiWeb over its REST API, without opening an SSH session:

  • Sessions: concurrent sessions and connection rate for the whole box.
  • Per-policy sessions: sessions, connections per second, client and server round-trip times, application response time, and the health of each backend pool member.
  • Throughput: for one policy or the whole box, charted in Mbps.
  • Transactions: HTTP transaction counts over time.

How they behave:

  • Thresholds are plain numbers, and the unit is shown for each type.
  • Discover from device has a new REST telemetry option.
  • Licence-locked boxes. These probes keep working on a FortiWeb whose configuration API is locked by a licence problem, which is exactly the case where the hourly configuration sync fails.
  • FortiWeb only. FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer are refused by name, so they are never shown as zero.

Traffic per appliance and per server policy#

Service Monitor opens with one traffic card per FortiWeb. Each card shows:

  • total throughput (average, peak and a small trend line)
  • box sessions, connection rate, CPU and memory
  • a table of the device's server policies with sessions, connections per second, throughput and backends up

Click a policy to open its full view. It shows the key figures, every backend pool member with its health, and the sessions, throughput and transactions trends side by side.

Both views are built only from stored samples. Opening them never contacts the appliance, so they work even when the box is off.

They never invent numbers:

  • A missing, disabled or never-run probe shows not measured, not 0.
  • Old samples are flagged with their age.
  • There is deliberately no single badge per device, because one healthy probe could hide three missing ones.

Collapsible device cards#

On Deep monitors and Service Monitor you can fold each device card, and the page remembers your choice.

  • A folded card still shows what matters: its status badge and a headline figure (average throughput or number of policies).
  • Keyboard. You can fold and unfold cards with the keyboard.
  • New look. The cards have a refreshed visual style.

Live server-policy picker#

When you create a probe, the policy name field suggests the policies the appliance reports live, not from cached data, which is empty on a licence-locked box. If the appliance cannot be asked, the form says so. "No policies" and "could not ask" no longer look the same.

Drill-down charts and two years of history#

  • Detailed charts. Click any small chart on the deep monitors to open a detailed chart for 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or a date range you choose. It shows min/average/max, the status strip, the percentage of time healthy, and the threshold lines.
  • Long history. SATOM now keeps hourly summaries for 90 days and daily summaries for two years, in under 400 KB per probe. Each summary keeps the highest and lowest value as well as the average, so a short spike stays visible.
  • The chart says what it drew. It tells you whether it shows raw samples, hourly or daily summaries, because an hourly average and a five-minute reading say different things.
  • No setup needed. History works on a fresh install without any scheduled action.

Alerts for automations that break#

A failing scheduled automation now raises its own alert. Before, an automation could fail run after run, or stop running altogether, without anyone being told. The alert looks at two things:

  • Repeated failures: how many scheduled runs in a row have failed.
  • Overdue runs: an enabled action that should have run long ago. A dead scheduler produces no failures to count, so this catches it.

Each action raises one alert, and a rise from warning to critical still gets through. Only scheduled runs count; a manual retry is already on your screen. A skipped run clears the count, so an action whose targets are all parked goes quiet. Two new settings in Settings → Alerts control this: Automation fail streak → critical and Automation overdue (hours).

Documentation and the public site#

  • The manual is linked from the sign-in page, so someone who cannot get in can still reach the installation guide, the console reference and the recovery runbooks without signing in.
  • The API manual is a top-level entry in the public site's navigation and footer.
  • The changelog is readable in three places: the repository, the application's Documentation section and the public site.
  • The manual is published from the same source as the repository. Its command table is generated from the console itself. Internal addresses, names and email addresses are replaced before publishing. If anything is left, publishing stops. Only documents on the list are published.
  • The public site has three colour themes: Aurora (the default, light), Abyss (dark) and Classic (SATOM's original colours). Pick one from the swatch in the navigation bar; your browser remembers it, and it applies before the page appears.

Installing on openSUSE#

  • New offline bundle for openSUSE and SLES 15. Installing on openSUSE used to need internet access, which an isolated management network does not have.
  • It is kept apart from the RHEL bundle, because the two are not interchangeable. Using the wrong bundle is refused before anything is changed.
  • The bundle is used without touching the system's own software sources, and nothing is left registered afterwards.

What changes for you#

  • Monitoring is in every ADOM. Fleet health, Metrics and Deep monitors now appear in the FortiWeb, FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer ADOMs as well as Global. Each ADOM sees only its own devices and probes. Anything created from Global for a device of that product appears there too.
  • Probes run every 3 minutes instead of 5.
  • CPU, memory and proxy daemon probes moved from 5 to 3 minutes. Interface and transactions probes stay at 15.
  • All intervals are now multiples of the sweep, so a probe does not silently drift to a slower rhythm.
  • Measured from start to finish, a probe actually runs about every 3.4 to 3.7 minutes.
  • Background work no longer opens a floating window.
  • Monitoring sweeps and the fleet hardware scan no longer show a progress pop-up with a Stop button.
  • The bell gets a notification only when they fail.
  • The Job Manager still shows them in full.
  • Discover from device still shows its progress, because you are waiting for the result.
  • Notifications from background work now belong to the right ADOM.
  • Probe now with nothing selected runs only the current page's probe types for the current ADOM's devices. On Deep monitors it no longer also runs the Service Monitor probes. In Global it still covers the whole fleet.
  • A scheduled monitoring sweep reports whether it ran, not whether it liked what it found. Before, one policy with all its backends down marked the sweep as failed until the backend was fixed. The worst status found now goes in the run's summary.
  • Device cards start folded and fit more on screen.
  • They are laid out in a dense grid, so a large fleet fits on one screen.
  • An opened card spans the full width.
  • Your earlier fold choices are not carried over; everything starts folded.
  • The proxy daemon probe shows memory used and free, in megabytes. It used to show a percentage that could exceed 100% and did not measure real memory use. Box memory thresholds remain the job of the memory probe.
  • Charts work without internet. The charting library is now served by SATOM itself instead of being downloaded from the internet.

Fixed#

Health, alerts and ADOMs#

  • The Fleet health badge could never turn red. Each device was graded only on capacity headroom, so even a powered-off appliance with no data showed green. The badge now combines four signals: recent harvests, the age of the cached data, enabled deep monitors and capacity. It has a separate unknown state, and the reasons are printed under it.
  • A red badge never sent mail. The device alert only checked whether the device answered on its port, so devices whose data collection had been failing for a week never triggered an email. The alert now uses the same signals as the badge, sends one alert per device listing every problem, and still gets through when a device gets worse. A new setting in Settings → Alerts sets the lowest status that sends mail: warning (the default) or critical.
  • Product ADOMs showed SATOM's own infrastructure. Fleet health showed node names, infrastructure addresses, the database and service cards, and encryption in transit inside the FortiWeb, FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer ADOMs. These sections are now shown only in Global, and product ADOMs cannot load them at all.
  • Two fleet-wide actions ignored the ADOM. Scan hardware on Fleet health and Probe now on Deep monitors, run with nothing selected, logged in to every device in the fleet, including other products' boxes. They now stay within the current ADOM. Global still covers the whole fleet.
  • The maintenance flag on the Monitoring device card was always off.
  • Maintenance stopped alerts but not work. A parked appliance was still swept by every automatic run and counted as a failure, which kept the action red. Automatic runs now skip parked appliances. A run whose targets are all parked reports skipped. A manual run still reaches them, because you park a box precisely to work on it.
  • Probes on a parked appliance no longer turn the monitoring summary red. They are still listed, under their own heading.

Monitoring#

  • The transactions probe could report zero for a busy policy. A real load test with about 2,700 requests per second showed zero transactions until a web protection profile was attached. The probe now double-checks whenever it reads zero, and warns if the policy is carrying traffic.
  • A "Working…" window with a dead Stop button kept reappearing. Test runs had been writing unfinished jobs into the live application. Leftover jobs are now cleaned up while SATOM runs, not only at start-up. A job that never started is considered dead after 10 minutes instead of an hour.
  • Device cards on the probe pages appeared as a grey block. They were drawn with dark-theme colours on SATOM's light pages, and status badges could be almost impossible to read. They now use SATOM's own colours.

Installation and HA#

  • An HA pair on openSUSE never copied files between nodes, along with five other problems found by installing a real pair:
  • Pasting the join key on the second node failed, because the key was read with a program that is not installed yet at that point. The key is now read without it, and both certificates in it are checked.
  • The remote login service was installed but not started on openSUSE, so the standby could never fetch data. It is now switched on on both nodes, since either may need to serve after a promotion.
  • A failed check of the peer's identity was ignored, which would have broken file copying for good while the installer reported success. It now warns and explains the fix. Database replication is not affected.
  • The standby's file-sync service failed but reported success. It now tells "could not check" apart from "nothing to sync".
  • The installer left files owned by the administrator in SATOM's own folders. This broke standby sync, certificate issuance and updates. A final ownership pass now runs before services start.
  • Seven installer problems, three of which affected every fresh install:
  • SATOM's settings file could not be read by the background services. On a new install the alert engine, certificate renewal, git publishing and HA sync could not run.
  • Git publishing reported failure on every new install before any device had been synced. It now finishes cleanly when there is nothing to publish.
  • Re-running the installer left the running services on the old passwords. Every login failed while the health check still passed. Services are now restarted.
  • On openSUSE the service account could join a shared group instead of its own.
  • On openSUSE several steps called a Python name that does not exist there.
  • On openSUSE the database rejected SATOM before even checking its password. The installer now writes its own access rule first. This also closes a gap on standalone installs on every Linux family.
  • On openSUSE the web server settings were loaded twice and clashed with the built-in default site.

The console and the public site#

  • The application showed version 1.0 for four releases. The footer and Settings → System Information now show the real version, and so does the public site.
  • The public API manual was readable without signing in and showed internal details, including a management host name and an internal address. Every public document is now cleaned before it is shown. If anything internal remains, the page is not served at all.
  • The sign-in pages and public documentation needed internet access to display properly. They now use files that ship with SATOM.
  • The site name in the navigation bar was almost invisible against the dark bar. Every text colour in all three themes now meets accessibility contrast standards.
  • The product logo had picked up a background plate and frame. It is transparent again.
  • The public pages had drifted apart. Navigation, footer and logo are now the same on every page, and the documentation pages no longer show an old placeholder logo or ignore the theme.
  • The in-app manual broke lines in the middle of sentences.

The operator console#

  • The console could crash while printing on a terminal that only supports plain ASCII, such as a serial console. Special characters are now replaced instead.
  • Two checks changed the files they were checking. They left files owned by the administrator in SATOM's folders, which another check then reported as a problem.
  • The database backup command wrote a file nothing could restore. It now writes the same backup bundle as System Backup & Restore. The backup status command also reported "no bundles" while twenty were on disk; this is fixed.
  • Rebuilding the Python environment could leave the node worse off on an isolated network, and it did not ask for confirmation. It now requires --yes. Every destructive command must ask for confirmation.
  • Display fixes:
  • columns that ran together in the command list
  • help text that was hard to pick out
  • stray trailing spaces when pasting
  • a missing line break after the ? list
  • Ctrl-C at the interactive prompt now clears the line instead of leaving the console.
  • diagnose all no longer repeats notes from checks that passed.

Before you upgrade#

  • Internal names change from the old product name to SATOM. The database, the database account, the Linux service account and the database certificate folder are renamed. New installations use the new names from the start. Existing installations migrate with the migration script that ships with this release. It takes a database dump first and checks health before reporting success. Three names are kept on purpose:
  • the Fortinet product names, which SATOM has to use
  • the database replication slot, which cannot be renamed safely under a live standby
  • the external backup server, which the appliances push to by name
  • Old proxy daemon samples are cleared. The probe now measures in megabytes instead of a percentage, so its earlier samples are removed rather than charted next to the new ones.

Under the hood#

  • Monitoring history uses very little disk: under 400 KB per probe for two years, against roughly 35 MB if raw samples were kept.
  • The public site and the in-app documentation now use one shared list of what may be published and how it is cleaned.
